history.yearNote: Wikipedia dates it to June or July 1827, although it is often given as 1826.
history.label: Niépce, View from the Window at Le Gras
history.note: The source only says ‘several days’, so the bar stops at three.

sources.name: Harry Ransom Center (holds the plate)
sources.quote: After several days of exposure to sunlight, the plate yielded an impression of the courtyard, outbuildings, and trees outside.

sources.name: Wikipedia: View from the Window at Le Gras
sources.quote: an exposure that lasted about eight hours, which has become the traditional estimate; however, a modern researcher who studied Niépce's notes and recreated his processes found that the exposure must have continued for several days

history.yearNote: According to Wikipedia, it was taken between 24 April and 4 May in either 1837 or 1838.
history.label: Daguerre: Boulevard du Temple
history.note: The sources disagree, so the bar covers both figures.

sources.name: Wikipedia: Boulevard du Temple (photograph)
sources.quote: by 1838, Daguerre had developed his own method whereby the exposure was reduced to only four to five minutes

sources.name: American Ancestors (NEHGS) Vita Brevis
sources.quote: due to the long exposure time of about ten to twelve minutes, all people in the photograph moved and avoided being captured

history.label: Early daguerreotypes
history.note: The two sources give different figures, so the bar covers both.

sources.name: Digital Public Library of America
sources.quote: Though early daguerreotype images required an exposure of around twenty minutes, by the early 1840s it had been reduced to about twenty seconds.

sources.name: Library of Congress (Cornelius self-portrait)
sources.quote: the daguerreotype process required a lengthy exposure that could take as long as thirty minutes

history.yearNote: The source says ‘early 1840s’, so I plotted it at 1842.
history.label: Daguerreotypes, early 1840s

sources.name: Digital Public Library of America
sources.quote: by the early 1840s it had been reduced to about twenty seconds

history.label: Talbot's calotype
history.note: Harvard’s timeline only says ‘seconds’, so the bar uses the more specific figure for bright sun.

sources.name: Wikipedia: Calotype
sources.quote: could be done in a minute or two if the subject was in bright sunlight

sources.name: Harvard Photograph Preservation Program timeline
sources.quote: reduced the necessary exposure time in the camera to seconds

history.label: Wet collodion
history.note: I plotted ‘a few seconds’ as three seconds.

sources.name: Science and Media Museum
sources.quote: Exposure times varied from a few seconds to a few minutes

sources.name: Royal Collection Trust
sources.quote: typically lasting only a few seconds

history.yearNote: The process was introduced in 1871 and went into general manufacture in 1878.
history.label: Gelatin dry plate
history.note: The source gives no number, so I plotted it as 1/50 s to 1 s.

sources.name: Science and Media Museum
sources.quote: By the 1870s, truly instantaneous photographs—with exposures of a fraction of a second—were possible

history.yearNote: The photographs were taken in June 1878.
history.label: Muybridge, The Horse in Motion
history.note: This figure was claimed at the time rather than measured.

sources.name: Wikipedia: The Horse in Motion (citing Sacramento Daily Union 18 June 1878)

history.yearNote: The Smithsonian American Art Museum dates the photograph to 1964.

sources.name: Smithsonian American Art Museum
